:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Solutions to Simple Harmonic Motion Equations

before.:question/problem:
A particle is moving with simple harmonic motion. The position of the particle $y(t)$ at time $t$ is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=0.
$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+{ϕ}_{1})$
II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}t+{ϕ}_{2})$
III. $y=A\operatorname{sec}⁡\sqrt{5}t+B\operatorname{csc}⁡\sqrt{5}t$

Note that $R,{ϕ}_{1},{ϕ}_{2},A$ and $B$ are constants.

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
The SHM equation is

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.
$$

The general solution to the SHM equation can be written in three different forms:

- $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+{ϕ}_{1})$

- $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+{ϕ}_{2})$

- $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t$

In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=5\,⟹\,\omega =\sqrt{5}.
$$

Thus, we have:

- $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}t+{ϕ}_{1})$

- $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}t+{ϕ}_{2})$

- $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{5}t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{5}t$

Therefore, only statement II could be used to represent $y(t).$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Divergent Sequences

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following sequences diverge?

I. ${a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{3}}{1-{n}^{2}}$ for $n\ge 2$
II. ${a}_{n}=\frac{3}{n}$ for $n\ge 1$
III. ${a}_{n}=\frac{2{n}^{2}-3{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}+5}$ for $n\ge 1$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Let's analyze each sequence in turn. We need to calculate the limit of each sequence as $n$ approaches infinity.

- In sequence I,  the dominant term in the denominator is $-{n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{3}}{1-{n}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{0-1} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

- In sequence II, the limit is

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{3}{n}=0.
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

- In sequence III, the dominant term in the denominator is ${n}^{3},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{3}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{2{n}^{2}-3{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}+5} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2{n}^{2}}{{n}^{3}}-\frac{3{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}})}{(\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}}+\frac{5}{{n}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2}{n}-3)}{(1+\frac{5}{{n}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{0-3}{1+0} \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

In conclusion, sequence I diverges.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Augmented Matrices in Row Echelon Form

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following augmented matrices have coefficient matrices that are **not** in row echelon form? Treat the final column of each augmented matrix as its constants column.

$$
A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
B=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 0 & 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 5\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
C=\left[\begin{array}{ccccc|c}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 & 1\end{array}\right].
$$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
A coefficient matrix, obtained by omitting the final column of its augmented matrix, is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The coefficient matrix of $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{array}\right]
$$

- The coefficient matrix of $B$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entries of its first two rows are in columns $3$ and $2,$ respectively (condition II is violated).

$$
B=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 0 & 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 5\end{array}\right]
$$

- The coefficient matrix of $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=\left[\begin{array}{ccccc|c}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 & 1\end{array}\right]
$$

Therefore, only $B$ has a coefficient matrix that is **not** in row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying the Orthogonality of a Two-Vector Set

before.:question/problem:
Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following are orthogonal sets?
- **U.** $U={Q(\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$
- **W.** $W={Q(\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix})}$
- **V.** $V={Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as 

$\,$ ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})},\,$ ${Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})},\,$ and $\,{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})}.$ 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=18-18=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=1-1=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthogonal.

- For the Set $V,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=2+12-5=9\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only".

before.:question/problem:
Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** If $\text{Ker}(T)={[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,y=z=0}$ then $\text{rank}(T)=2$
- **II.** If $Tx=[1,0,0]^{T}$ has more than one solution, then $\text{nullity}(T)=0$
- **III.** If $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}$, then $T$ is invertible
before.:question/worked-solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since $y=z=0,$ any vector from $\text{Ker}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=x\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{v}_{1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=1.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T) & =3-\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $Tx=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ has more than one solution, there are ${u}_{1},{u}_{2}\in {R}^{3}$ such that  ${u}_{1}\ne {u}_{2}$ and 

$$
T({u}_{1})=T({u}_{2})=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means, $T$ is not a bijection and according to the invertible matrix theorem, $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$

- Statement III is false. Notice that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=1.$ So, $T$ is not a bijection or, which is the same, $T$ is not invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

*If  $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$, then $\underline{\phantom{xxxxxx}}.$ * 

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?
- **I.** $\text{rank}(T)=4$
- **II.** $\text{nullity}(T)=4$
- **III.** $T$ is a bijection

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{5}$ into ${R}^{5},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=5 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=5.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ and the set ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent, we get that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=4.$

- Statement II is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =5-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =5-4 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct option is "I only."

before.:question/problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3},w}$ is linearly independent
- **II.** ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is linearly dependent
- **III.** ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}$ is a basis of $V$

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** **If** $12$ is divisible by $3$, **then** $9$ is divisible by $4.$
- **II.** **If** $5$ is divisible by $2$, **then** $10$ is divisible by $5.$
- **III.** **If** $9$ is divisible by $5$, **then** $6$ is divisible by $3.$
before.:question/worked-solution:
An implication $A⇒B$ is true *unless* $A$ is true and $B$ is false. In other words, the implication is true unless the "promise" is broken.

- Statement I is false. The antecedent "$12$ is divisible by $3$" is true, and the consequent "$9$ is divisible by $4$" is false. So the promise is broken, and the statement is false.

- Statement II is true. The antecedent "$5$ is divisible by $2$" is false, so the promise does not apply. Regardless of the consequent, the promise is *not* broken, and the statement is true.

- Statement III is true. Again, the antecedent "$9$ is divisible by $5$" is false, so the promise does not apply. Regardless of the consequent, the promise is *not* broken, and the statement is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:topic/_knowledge-points.:topic/title: Type I and II Regions in Two-Dimensional Space

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the finite region bounded between the curves $y={x}^{3}$ and $y=\sqrt[3]{x},$ in the first quadrant?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** It is a type I region
- **II.** It is a type II region
- **III.** It's neither a type I nor a type II region
before.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}y={x}^{3}\, & ⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y} \\ y=\sqrt[3]{x}\, & ⟹\,x={y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/89/899357795c6d5b81d3cb619d71493ad787645697fe1f2fcecda78c1b875f388e.png)

We have the following:

- Any vertical line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le \sqrt[3]{x}}.
$$

So, this is a type I region.

- Any horizontal line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,{y}^{3}\le x\le \sqrt[3]{y}}.
$$

So, this is a type II region.

Therefore, only statements I and II are true.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Truth Value of a Statement Involving Nested Quantifiers

before.:question/problem:
Let $p\in Q$ and $q\in Q.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $∃\,p\in Q,\,2p=-1.$
- **II.** The truth set of the predicate $(\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1\,)$ is $Q.$
- **III.** $∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1.$
before.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the statement 

$$
∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1
$$

from option III reads as follows:

$\,$ There exist rationals $q$ and $p,$ such that $p\cdot q=-1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true, $2p=-1$ for some rational number $p$ (e.g., for $p=-\frac{1}{2}$).

- Statement II is false. For the predicate

$$
P(q):\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1
$$

we note that $P(q)$ is true for some $q\in Q$ and false for others. For example, 

$$
P(0):\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot 0=-1
$$

is false. However, 

$$
P(1):\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot 1=-1
$$

is true, since we can take $p=-1.$

- Statement III is true. The sentence 

$$
(\,∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1\,)
$$

 
can be written as

$$
∃q\in Q\,(\,\underbrace{∃p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1}_{P(q)}\,)
$$

which is true whenever the inner predicate $P(q)$ has a nonempty truth set. And according to the discussion in statement II, this is the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:topic/_knowledge-points.:topic/title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A)$ for every matrix $A?$
- **I.** $\text{Col}({A}^{T})$
- **II.** $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$
- **III.** $\text{Null}(A)$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ consists of all linear combinations of the columns of $A$, that is, the rows of ${A}^{T}.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of ${A}^{T},$ it must be orthogonal to each row of ${A}^{T}.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by ${A}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${A}^{T}$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}(A)$ must be orthogonal to the left null space of $A,$ which is $\text{Null}({A}^{T}).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](images/de/de22dd5b352e1d5be48f4b6ed3b2a4657ae623c1bd288d3464559758ea334af7.png)

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following are logically equivalent to $R?$
- **I.** $(T∨R)∧T$
- **II.** $R∧(T∨R)$
- **III.** $(R∨T)∧R$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
The law that conjunction absorbs disjunction is stated as

$$
R∧(R∨T)≡R.
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement I is *not* logically equivalent to $R.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}(T∨R)∧T & ≡T∧(T∨R) \\  & ≡T≢R.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is logically equivalent to $R.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}R∧(T∨R) & ≡R∧(R∨T) \\  & ≡R.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is logically equivalent to $R.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}(R∨T)∧R & ≡R∧(R∨T) \\  & ≡R.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Which of the following statements must be true for any integers $x$ and $y?$

- **I.** $2∣(60x-45y)$

- **III.** $5∣(60x-45y)$
before.:question/worked-solution:
The notation $a∣b$ means $a$ divides $b.$

According to the definition of integer divisibility, the fact that $a$ divides $b$ means that there exists an integer $k$ such that 

$$
b=ak.
$$

 
With that in mind, let's examine our statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, if $x=0$ and $y=1,$ we have $60(0)-45(1)=-45,$ which is not divisible by $2.$

- Statement III is true. Notice that 

$$
60x-45y=5(12x-9y).
$$

Since $x$ and $y$ are integers, $12x-9y$ must be an integer, too. So, $5∣(60x-45y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is " III only."

before.:question/problem:
Consider the following predicates.

$\,$ $A(x):$ $x\in Z.$ $\,$ $B(x):$ $-x\in Z.$

Which of the following is equivalent to the biconditional predicate $A(x)⇔B(x)?$

I. If $x\in Z$ then $-x\in Z$, and if $-x\in Z$ then $x\in Z.$

before.:question/worked-solution:
A biconditional expression $P⇔Q≡(P⇒Q)∧(Q⇒P)$ can be read as shown below:

- $P$ if and only if $Q$

- $P$ is equivalent to $Q$

- If $P$ then $Q,$ and if $Q$ then $P$

So, $A⇔B$ translates into the following sentences:

- $x\in Z$ if and only if $-x\in Z.$

- $x\in Z$ is equivalent to $-x\in Z.$

- If $x\in Z$ then $-x\in Z$, and if $-x\in Z$ then $x\in Z.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

:topic/_knowledge-points.:topic/title: The Divergence of a Vector Field

before.:question/problem:
![](images/58/584016c88e5916984e181118d52caab95dba1fd0d861e0fd248a4e023d1b07da.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{div}\,F=0$
- **II.** $\text{div}\,F>0$
- **III.** $\text{div}\,F<0$
- **IV.** $F$ is solenoidal
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement III is true, whereas statements I and II are false. Notice that the lengths of the vectors decrease as we move horizontally and vertically towards the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a sink at every point.

- Statement IV is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

before.:question/problem:
$\,$ **If** $-2\in Z,$ **then** $5$ is prime.

Which of the following statements are equivalent to the conditional statement above?
- **I.** If $-2\notin Z,$ then $5$ is not prime.
- **II.** If $5$ is prime, then $-2\in Z.$
- **III.** If $5$ is not prime, then $-2\notin Z.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Let's recall the following facts:

- The contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original statement.

- The inverse and the converse are logically equivalent to each other, but not to the original statement.

![](images/0d/0deb19675402bf931111bb80cb616682aac08491b5cd3e1ab5812da05b6df8a8.png)

So, we are looking for the contrapositive of the given statement.

- Statement I is the inverse, not the contrapositive. $\,\times $

- Statement II is the converse, not the contrapositive. $\,\times $

- Statement III is the contrapositive. $\,✓$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:topic/_knowledge-points.:topic/title: Linear Independence in Abstract Vector Spaces

before.:question/problem:
Consider a vector space $V$ and vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}\in V.$ Given that ${{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly independent set and ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},\text{ }{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly dependent one, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${v}_{1}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{2}$, ${v}_{3}$ and ${v}_{4}$
- **II.** ${v}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{3}$ and ${v}_{4}$
- **III.** ${v}_{2}+{v}_{3}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{4}$
before.:question/worked-solution:
Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly dependent set, we obtain that

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

has a non-zero solution. Moreover, ${x}_{1}$ can't be zero because then

$$
{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

will have a non-zero solution and that's a contradiction as ${{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent.
Therefore, from ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0,$ we get

$$
{v}_{1}=-\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}{v}_{2}-\frac{{x}_{3}}{{x}_{1}}{v}_{3}-\frac{{x}_{4}}{{x}_{1}}{v}_{4}.
$$

This means that ${v}_{1}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{2}$, ${v}_{3},$ and ${v}_{4}.$

- Statement II is false. Since ${{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly independent set, ${v}_{2}$ can not be a linear combination of other vectors.

- Statement III is false. Since ${{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly independent set, ${v}_{3}$ can not be a linear combination of ${v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{4}.$ As a result ${v}_{2}+{v}_{3}$ can't be written as combination of ${v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{4}$ too.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

before.:question/problem:
$\,$ $P(y):$ $y<y+1⇒{y}^{-1}\in Q.$

Given that the above predicate is defined over the universal set ${Z}^{-},$ which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** The truth set of $P(y)$ is $∅.$
- **II.** The truth set of $P(y)$ is ${Z}^{-}.$
- **III.** $∀y\in {Z}^{-},\,P(y).$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
before.:question/worked-solution:
The *universal quantification* of a predicate $P(x),$ defined over the universal set $U,$ transforms this predicate into a statement that we write as

$$
∀x\in U,\,P(x).
$$

This statement is true if the predicate $P(x)$ is true on the entire universal set $U,$ i.e. if the truth set ${T}_{P}$ of the predicate coincides with the universal set $U:$

$$
{T}_{P}=U
$$

First, notice that:

- the truth set of "$y<y+1$" is ${Z}^{-},$ and

- the truth set of "${y}^{-1}\in Q$" is ${Z}^{-}.$

Since $A⇒B≡¬A∨B,$ the truth set of our predicate is 

$$
{T}_{P}=\overset{―}{{Z}^{-}}\cup {Z}^{-}=∅\cup {Z}^{-}={Z}^{-}.
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement I is false. The truth set is *not* empty.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, ${T}_{P}={Z}^{-}.$

- Statement III is true. Since ${T}_{P}$ coincides with the universal set, the statement $∀y\in {Z}^{-},\,P(y)$ is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Given that the above predicate is defined over the universal set $Z,$ which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** The truth set of $P(m)$ is $∅.$
- **II.** The truth set of $P(m)$ is ${2k:k\in Z}.$
- **III.** $∀m\in Z,\,P(m).$

{T}_{P}=U

before.:question/problem:
$\,$ $P(n):$ $n$ is odd or $n+1$ is odd

Given that the above predicate is defined over the universal set $N,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The truth set of $P(n)$ is $∅.$
- **II.** The truth set of $P(n)$ is $N.$
- **III.** $∃n\in N,\,P(n).$
before.:question/worked-solution:
The *existential quantification* of a predicate $P(x),$ defined over the universal set $U,$ transforms this predicate into a statement that we write as

$$
∃x\in U,\,P(x).
$$

This statement is true if the predicate $P(x)$ is true for a single element $x\in U,$ i.e. if the truth set ${T}_{P}$ of the predicate is not empty:

$$
{T}_{P}\ne ∅
$$

First, notice that:

- the truth set of "$n$ is odd" is the set of odd natural numbers, and

- the truth set of "$n+1$ is odd" is the set of even natural numbers.

So, the truth set of our predicate is

$$
{T}_{P}={\text{odd natural numbers}}\cup {\text{even natural numbers}}=N.
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement I is false. The truth set is *not* empty.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, ${T}_{P}=N.$

- Statement III is true. Since ${T}_{P}$ is *not* empty, the statement $∃n\in N,\,P(n)$ is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions

:topic/_knowledge-points.:topic/title: Limits and Continuity of Multivariable Functions

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}
$$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{3}$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$
- **II.** The limit evaluates to $-1$ along the path $y=-{x}^{2}$
- **III.** The limit exists and is equal to $\frac{1}{3}$
before.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}=\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+2\cdot 0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-{x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-{x}^{2}}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2(-{x}^{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-{x}^{2}}{-{x}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}=\text{DNE}
$$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Injections For Functions Whose Domain or Codomain Are Real Intervals

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $f:[-2,4]\to [-3,9]$ which is given by $f(x)=2x+1?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $f(-2)=f(4)$
- **II.** $∀\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in [-2,4],$ if $f({x}_{1})=f({x}_{2}),$ we have ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}$
- **III.** $f$ is an injection
before.:question/worked-solution:
First, we graph the function.

![](images/5f/5fd931a87d6a5fb32d10ed931f443a8175f0760eba9fe2fe69336f8f79e9fd68.png)

A function $f:X\to Y$ is an injection (also known as *one-to-one*) if *every* element in $X$ is mapped to a *distinct* element in $Y:$ 

$f:X\to Y$ is an injection if $∀\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in X,$ if $f({x}_{1})=f({x}_{2}),$ we have ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have $f(2)=2(-2)+1=-3$ and $f(4)=2\cdot 4+1=9.$

- Statement II is true. As we can see from the graph, it passes the horizontal line test, meaning that there are no two distinct elements within $[-2,4]$ that map to the same element in $[-3,9].$ So, for all ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ contained within the domain $[-2,4],$ if $f({x}_{1})$ and $f({x}_{2})$ are equal, then we must have ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since statement II is true, $f$ is an injection.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

- **II.** $g:R\to R$ defined by $g(x)=(x-2)^{2}$
- **III.** $h:R\to R$ defined by $h(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$

$f:X\to Y$ is an injection if $∀\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in X,$ if $f({x}_{1})=f({x}_{2}),$ we have ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$

$$

- III is *not* an injection. For example, $h(0)=1=h(2\pi ),$ but $0\ne 2\pi .$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

before.:question/problem:
$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{{x}^{8}},\, & x\ge 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Given the function $f(x)$ above, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\ge 1$
- **II.** ${\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$
- **III.** $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function
before.:question/worked-solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for $x\ge 1,$ we have $f(x)=\frac{7}{{x}^{8}}\ge 0.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{7}{{x}^{8}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{7}}\,{|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statements I and II are true, the first and second conditions are satisfied. So, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

before.:question/problem:
Given that $26≡8\,(\text{mod}\,n),$ which of the following could be the value of $n?$
- **I.** $n=9$
- **II.** $n=8$
- **III.** $n=3$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
First, we recall that 

$$
a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,n∣(a-b).
$$

So, $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $(a-b)$ is divisible by $n$ (there is no remainder).

We have $a-b=26-8=18.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Note that $9∣18$ because $18÷9=2,$ and there is no remainder. Therefore, the statement is true when $n=9.$

- Note that $8∤18.$ Therefore, the statement is false when $n=8.$

- Note that $3∣18$ because $18÷3=6,$ and there is no remainder. Therefore, the statement is true when $n=3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Whether Two Integers are Coprime

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{gcd}(765,221)=17$
- **II.** $\text{gcd}(765,221)=1$
- **III.** $765$ and $221$ are coprime
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that two integers are coprime if their greatest common divisor is $1.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Indeed, let's use the Euclidean algorithm, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}765 & = & 221\cdot 3 & + & 102 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 221 & = & 102\cdot 2 & + & 17 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 102 & = & 17\cdot 6 & + & 0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

The last positive remainder is $17.$ So, the greatest common divisor of $765$ and $221$ is $17:$

$$
\text{gcd}(765,221)=17.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{gcd}(765,221)>1,$ the numbers are not coprime.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined
before.:question/worked-solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,\sqrt{3})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,-1)$

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined
before.:question/worked-solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(1,-1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)}}=-{e}^{\sqrt{-1}}
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}={e}^{1}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=-\frac{e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot \frac{{e}^{\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}}{2\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}=\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II  only'.

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A⇒¬B≡¬(A∧B)$
- **II.** $¬(A⇒¬B)≡A∧B$
- **III.** $¬(A⇒¬B)≡¬A∧B$
before.:question/worked-solution:
Let's examine each of our statements:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $A⇒¬B$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $¬A∨¬B,$ which by De Morgan's law is equivalent to $¬(A∧B).$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. From part I, we have the following equivalence:

$$
A⇒¬B≡¬(A∧B)
$$

By negating this statement, we get

$$
¬(A⇒¬B)≡¬(¬(A∧B)).
$$

Canceling out double negation, we reach

$$
A∧B.
$$

So, $¬(A⇒¬B)$ is equivalent to $A∧B.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:topic/_knowledge-points.:topic/title: The Curl of a Vector Field

before.:question/problem:
![](images/17/17637e938a25e91b9a03921dbbe0f22c8ea760f09cfed9b4a76d07bd5e3b9301.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{curl}\,F=0$
- **II.** $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$
- **III.** $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the negative $z$-direction.
- **IV.** $F$ is irrotational
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

![](images/f3/f385add60afac473a5734f8c1ed57c6575bada03c9c16b24fed73b200c38e2c5.png)

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following sets are neither open nor closed?
- **I.** ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,0<{y}^{2}\le 5}$
- **II.** ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<7}$
- **III.** ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,1\le x<4,\,{y}^{2}<9}$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Let's examine our sets in turn.

- The first set is *neither open nor closed*. It contains some of its boundary points, for example, the point $(2,\sqrt{5}).$ On the other hand, it does not contain some other boundary points, for example, the point $(3,0).$

- The second set is *open* since it doesn't contain any of its boundary points (the corresponding inequality is strict).

- The third set is *neither open nor closed*. It contains some of its boundary points, for example, the point $(1,0).$ On the other hand, it does not contain some other boundary points, for example, the point $(4,0).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

before.:question/problem:
Given that ${1}_{A}(q)=0,$ which of the following statements about $\overset{―}{A}$ are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${1}_{\overset{―}{A}}\,(q)=1$

- **II.** ${1}_{\overset{―}{A}}\,(q)=0$

- **III.** $q\in \overset{―}{A}$

*Hint: ${1}_{A}$ denotes the indicator function of the set $A$ and ${1}_{\overset{―}{A}}$ denotes the indicator function of the complement of $A.$*
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the indicator functions of $\overset{―}{A},$ $A\cap B,$ and $A\cup B$ have the following properties:

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{\overset{―}{A}}\,(x) & =1-{1}_{A}(x) \\ {1}_{A\,\cap \,B}\,(x) & =min\{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)\} \\ {1}_{A\,\cup \,B}\,(x) & =max\{{1}_{A}(x),{1}_{B}(x)\}\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true while statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}_{\overset{―}{A}}\,(q) & =1-{1}_{A}(q) \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since ${1}_{\overset{―}{A}}\,(q)=1,$ we conclude that $q$ belongs to $\overset{―}{A}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $f:R\to R$ which is given by $f(x)=2-{x}^{2}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The range of $f$ is $(-\infty ,-2]$

- **II.** $∀\,y\in (-\infty ,2],$ $∃\,x\in R$ such that $f(x)=y$

- **III.** $f$ maps $R$ **into** $R$
before.:question/worked-solution:
First, we graph the function.

![](images/35/3575afe4fd4e5aa6754496154986b272a43fb5c035ec8d69621d52fad16ee1ea.png)

Recall that $f:X\to Y$ is an *into* function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element $y$ in $Y$ such that it has no preimage in $X:$ 

$f:X\to Y$ is an into function if $∃\,y\in Y$ such that $∀\,x\in X,$ we have $f(x)\ne y.$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. From the graph, the highest $y$-value is $2,$ and it occurs at the point $(0,2).$ The graph will cover all $y$-values lower than $y=2$, including $y=2$ itself. So the range of the function is $(-\infty ,2].$

- Statement II is true. Since the range of the function is $(-\infty ,2]$, then for all $y$ contained within $(-\infty ,2],$ there exists some $x$ contained within $R$ such that $f(x)=y.$

- Statement III is true. As we can see from the range, there is no real number $x$ such that $f(x)=3\in R.$ So, $f$ maps $R$ *into* $R.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields are conservative on ${R}^{2}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $F=\frac{2x}{{e}^{y}}\,i-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{y}}\,j$
- **II.** $G=\operatorname{arctan}⁡y\,i-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}+1}\,j$
- **III.** $H=(8x-3y)\,i+(4y-3x+1)\,j$
before.:question/worked-solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D={R}^{2}.$ With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields. 

- For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=\frac{2x}{{e}^{y}}$ and $Q=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{y}}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{2x}{{e}^{y}},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-\frac{2x}{{e}^{y}}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $G,$ we have $P=\operatorname{arctan}⁡y$ and $Q=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}+1}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $G$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $H,$ we have $P=8x-3y$ and $Q=4y-3x+1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-3.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $H$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following functions are bijections?
- **I.** $f:R\to R$ defined by $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x$
- **II.** $g:R\to R$ defined by $g(x)=2x$
- **III.** $h:Z\to Z$ defined by $h(x)=2x$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a function $f:X\to Y$ is a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

- I is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Remember that the range of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡x$ is $(-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).$ This means that 

$$
-\frac{\pi }{2}<\operatorname{arctan}⁡x<\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, for example, there is no value $x\in R$ such that $f(x)=4.$

- II is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $∀\,y\in R,$ we can choose an $x\in R$ such that $g(x)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =y \\ 2x & =y \\ x & =\frac{y}{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

We verify that

$$
g(x)=g(\frac{y}{2})=2(\frac{y}{2})=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}g({x}_{1}) & =g({x}_{2}) \\ 2{x}_{1} & =2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $g$ is both surjective and injective, $g$ is bijective.

- III is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Notice that if $x$ is an integer number, then $h(x)=2x$ is an even number. This means that the range of $h$ is the set of even numbers.
So, for example, there is no value $x\in Z$ such that $h(x)=3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A⇒B≡¬A∨B$
- **II.** $¬(A⇒B)≡A∨¬B$
- **III.** $¬(A⇒B)≡A∧¬B$
before.:question/worked-solution:
Let's examine each of our statements:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $A⇒B$ is logically equivalent to the disjunction $¬A∨B.$

- Statement III is true, while statement II is false. From part I, we have the following equivalence:

$$
A⇒B≡¬A∨B
$$

By negating this statement, we get

$$
¬(A⇒B)≡¬(¬A∨B).
$$

Distributing the negation over the disjunction using De Morgan's law, we have

$$
¬(¬A∨B)≡¬(¬A)∧¬B.
$$

Canceling out double negation, we reach

$$
A∧¬B.
$$

So, $¬(A⇒B)$ is equivalent to $A∧¬B.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:topic/_knowledge-points.:topic/title: The Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1.$
- **II.** $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5.$
- **III.** If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3,$ then $2v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-3.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-1\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-1v.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (but not $1$).

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{v}_{1} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-4\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-4{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=-4v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-4$ (but not $5$).

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(2v)=2Av=2(-3v)=-3(2v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(2v)=-3(2v),$ and $2v\ne 0,$ this implies that $2v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

before.:question/problem:
Consider the following set:

$$
A={{0},{0,1}}
$$

Given the relation $R$ on $A$ defined by

$$
X\,R\,Y\,⇔\,X⊃Y,
$$

which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${0}\,R\,{0,1}$
- **II.** ${0,1}\,R\,{0,1}$
- **III.** ${0}\,\cancel{\,R\,}\,{0}$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
before.:question/worked-solution:
A relation $R$ on a set $A$ is a subset of the Cartesian product $A\times A={A}^{2}.$

$$
R⊂{A}^{2}
$$

We also have the following notations:

- $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $(x,y)\in R$

- $x\,\cancel{\,R\,}\,y$ if and only if $(x,y)\notin R$

In this case, we have $X\,R\,Y$ if and only if $X⊃Y.$ For this relation, note that

- the symbols $R$ and $⊃$ are interchangeable, and

- the symbols $\cancel{\,R\,}$ and $⊅$ are also interchangeable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Replacing $R$ with the symbol $⊃,$ we have ${0}⊃{0,1}.$ This is equivalent to ${0,1}⊂{0},$ which is false.

- Statement II is false. Replacing $R$ with the symbol $⊃,$ we have ${0,1}⊃{0,1}.$ This is equivalent to ${0,1}⊂{0,1},$ which is false.

- Statement III is true. Replacing $\cancel{\,R\,}$ with the symbol $⊅,$ we have ${0}⊅{0}.$ This is equivalent to ${0}⊄{0},$ which is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following random variables could be modeled as a binomial distribution?
- **I.** The number of students who got an $A$ on a math exam in a class of $25$ students
- **II.** The number of cards drawn until a red card is obtained
- **III.** The number of books published by a publishing house in a month

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
A binomial distribution models the number of successes in a sequence of $n$ independent experiments (where each outcome is either success or failure).

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given random variables.

- Random variable I could be modeled as a binomial distribution. The number of students who got an $A$ on a math exam can be interpreted as the number of successes in a sequence of $25$ independent experiments.

- Random variable II could *not* be modeled as a binomial distribution. Although drawing a red card can be interpreted as a "success," there is not a fixed number of trials in this experiment.

- Random variable III could *not* be modeled as a binomial distribution. The number of books published cannot be interpreted as "success" or "failure."

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

before.:question/problem:
$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.3 & 0.8 \\ 0.7 & 0.2\end{bmatrix},\,q=\begin{bmatrix}0.1 \\ 0.9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $q$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $q$ is a stochastic vector
- **II.** $Pq=q$
- **III.** $q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that $Pq=q.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

- Statement II is false. Note that

$$
Pq=\begin{bmatrix}0.3 & 0.8 \\ 0.7 & 0.2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.1 \\ 0.9\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0.03+0.72 \\ 0.07+0.18\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0.75 \\ 0.25\end{bmatrix}\ne q.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $Pq\ne q,$ it is not a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Spectral Theorem

before.:question/problem:
Given that $A$ is a real symmetric matrix, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A$ must have a complex eigenvalue

- **II.** $A$ is not diagonalizable

- **III.** If $u$ and $v$ are two eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues, then $u⊥v$
before.:question/worked-solution:
Given that $A$ is an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix over $R$, the spectral theorem states the following:

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.

- Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

- $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the spectral theorem, the eigenvalues are real.

- Statement II is false. According to the spectral theorem, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable, so, $A$ is diagonalizable.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

before.:question/problem:
$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0$

II. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2}),Q({u}_{3})\}$ is orthogonal

III. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2}),Q({u}_{3})\}$ is orthonormal

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false since

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=3\ne 0.
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})⊥̸Q({u}_{3})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{3})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}\ne 0.
$$

- Statement III is false since the set is not even orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

before.:question/problem:
Given that $7≡19\,(\text{mod}\,n),$ which of the following could be the value of $n?$
- **I.** $n=5$
- **II.** $n=6$
- **III.** $n=7$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
First, we recall that 

$$
a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,n∣(a-b).
$$

So, $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $(a-b)$ is divisible by $n$ (there is no remainder).

We have $a-b=7-19=-12.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Note that $5∤(-12).$ Therefore, the statement is false when $n=5.$

- Note that $6∣(-12)$ because $(-12)÷6=-2,$ and there is no remainder. Therefore, the statement is true when $n=6.$

- Note that $7∤(-12).$ Therefore, the statement is false when $n=7.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

before.:question/problem:
Given that $det(A)=14$, and $I$ is the $3\times 3$ identity matrix, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{det}(A)-\text{det}(3I)=-13$

- **II.** $-\text{det}({A}^{T})+\text{det}(I)=-13$

- **III.** $\text{det}(A)-\text{det}({A}^{T})=-28$
before.:question/worked-solution:
From the properties of determinants, we know that 

$$
\text{det}({A}^{T})=\text{det}(A)=14
$$

and

$$
det(I)=1.
$$

Now, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}3I & =3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of a diagonal matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} & ={3}^{3}=27.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
\text{det}(A)-\text{det}(3I)=14-27=-13
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
-\text{det}({A}^{T})+\text{det}(I)=-14+1=-13
$$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\text{det}(A)-\text{det}({A}^{T})=14-14=0\ne -28
$$

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and II only".

before.:question/problem:
Let 
$A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.$
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The lines $5x-4y=0$ and $x+2y=0$ intersect at exactly one point
- **II.** ${A}^{-1}$ does **not** exist
- **III.** $Ax=0$ has no solution
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det\begin{bmatrix}5 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =5\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot 1 \\  & =14\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. 

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is true by the fourth part of  the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement II is false by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is false. According to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, the system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

Therefore, only statement I is true.

before.:question/problem:
Suppose ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are both solutions of the homogeneous system
${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t).$
Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same system?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $x(t)={x}_{1}(t)\times {x}_{2}(t)$

- **II.** $x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot {x}_{2}(t)$

- **III.** $x(t)=-3\cdot {x}_{2}(t)$
before.:question/worked-solution:
The *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system, then for any constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ the linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)
$$

is also a solution of the system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expressions.

- Option I might be *not* a solution to the system since it's not a scalar multiple of any of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

- Option II might be *not* a solution to the system since it's not a scalar multiple of any of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ Notice that the multiplier is not a constant.

- Option III is a solution to the system. Indeed, notice that

$$
-3\cdot {x}_{2}(t)
$$

is a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ with constant multiplies ${c}_{1}=0$ and ${c}_{2}=-3,$ respectively.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
v\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }w\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A+3I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps, 
the vector $v$ is a generalized  eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A.$

- Statement II is false. Since

$$
u\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }v\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }w\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A+3I$ maps $u$ to $0$ in $3$ steps, 
the vector $u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3,$ not $2.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since

$$
y\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-3I$ maps $y$ to $0$ in $1$ step, 
the vector $y$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $v$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $v$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- **II.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- **III.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$

before.:question/worked-solution:
A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{2}$ of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{1}\ne 0.$ Recall that an *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With this in mind, let's examine our statements.

First, we compute $A-2I:$

$$
A-2I=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)w=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}_{v}\overset{\,A-2I\,\,}{\to }\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}}_{w}\overset{\,A-2I\,\,}{\to }\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A-2I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps.

Therefore:

$\,$ *$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A.$*

So, the correct answer is "III only."

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?
- **I.** ${\int }_{-6}^{6}x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
- **II.** ${\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
- **III.** ${\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Hence, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

before.:question/problem:
Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

- **II.** $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$

- **III.** $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$
before.:question/worked-solution:
Since $f$ is the $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodicity:

$$
f(x)=F(x)
$$

 
for all $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

- Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodic, because for any $x\in R,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(x+\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x+2\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) \\  & =F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R.$

- Statement III is true. Since $f$ has period $\frac{\pi }{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+2\pi )=f(x+4\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})=f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

\begin{aligned}F(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(x+\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x+2\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) \\  & =F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R.$

- Statement “$f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$” is true. Since $f$ has period $\frac{\pi }{2},$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+2\pi )=f(x+4\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})=f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$”; “$f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$”; “$f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$”.

before.:question/problem:
Let $G(x)=x+1$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $g(x)$ is the $4$-periodic extension of $G(x)$ from $x\in [0,4)$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $g(x+8)=g(x)$ for all $x\in R$

- **II.** $g(x)=G(x)$ for all $x\in R$

- **III.** $g(x+2)=g(x)$ for all $x\in R$
before.:question/worked-solution:
Since $g$ is the $4$-periodic extension of $G,$ we have 

- $g(x+4)=g(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $g(x)=G(x)$ for all $x\in [0,4).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x+8)=g((x+4)+4)=g(x+4)=g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=5.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}g(5)=g(1+4)=g(1)=G(1)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}G(5)=5+1=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $g(x)\ne G(x)$ for $x=5.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=1.$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(1+2)=g(3)=G(3)=4\end{aligned}
$$

while 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(1)=G(1)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $g(x+2)\ne g(x)$ for $x=1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following systems of linear ODEs are decoupled?
- **I.** $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=4{x}_{1}(t)+5{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$
- **II.** $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-2{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &={x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$
- **III.** $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-7{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=9{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
before.:question/worked-solution:
A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently. 

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

- System I is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)+5{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System II is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{2}(t)$ and ${x}_{1}(t).$

- System III is decoupled since its equations depend on only one variable each. Indeed, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-7{x}_{1}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=9{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{2}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

before.:question/problem:
|  | $✠$ | $♣$ | $♠$ |

| $✠$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $♣$ | $1$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $♠$ | $0$ | $1$ | $1$ |

The adjacency matrix of the relation $R,$ defined on the set $\{✠,♣,♠\},$ is given above. Which of the following ordered pairs belong to the relation?

I. $(✠,♣)$

II. $(♣,♠)$

III. $(♠,✠)$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
If a relation $R$ is defined over $A=\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},…,{a}_{m}\}$ and $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},…{b}_{n}\}$ of cardinalities $m$ and $n,$ respectively, the *adjacency matrix* of $R$ is a $m\times n$-matrix (or table), where the element ${r}_{ij}$ at the intersection of the $i$th row and the $j$th column is given by

$$
{r}_{ij}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,\text{if }{a}_{i}\,R\,{b}_{j}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine the given ordered pairs.

- The pair $(✠,♣)$ belongs to the relation. Indeed, the adjacency matrix has $1$ on the intersection of the $✠$-row and the $♣$-column.

- The pair $(♣,♠)$ does not belong to the relation since the adjacency matrix has $0$ on the intersection of the $♣$-row and the $♠$-column.

- The pair $(♠,✠)$ does not belong to the relation since the adjacency matrix has $0$ on the intersection of the $♠$-row and the $✠$-column.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

before.:question/problem:
Given the two planes $x+y+z=0$ and $x+y+1=0$, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $⟨1,1,0⟩.$

- **II.** The planes intersect on a line.

- **III.** The planes are coincident.
before.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that:

- For the plane $x+y+z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,1,1⟩.$

- For the plane $x+y+1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,1,0⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,1,1⟩\times ⟨1,1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1,0⟩\ne ⟨1,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel. Hence, the corresponding planes must intersect on a line.

- Statement III is false. Indeed, two non-parallel planes could not be coincident either.

Therefore, only statement II is true.

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 & 5 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 9 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since ${a}_{32}\ne 0$ (condition  II is violated). 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 & 5 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

- The matrix $B$ is not in row echelon form since ${b}_{21}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 9 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, only $C$ is in row echelon form.

- **II.** $(10,20)$
- **III.** $(15,35)$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+5y & =200 \\ 2\cdot 15+5\cdot 35 & =200 \\ 30+175 & =200 \\ 205 & \ne 200\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Whether a Linear Diophantine Equation Has a Solution

before.:question/problem:
Which of the following Diophantine equations have solutions?
- **I.** $15x-20y=5$
- **II.** $11x+9y=13$
- **III.** $-8x+2y=5$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

has a solution if and only if $d\,|\,c,$ where $d=\text{gcd}(a,b).$  

With that in mind, let's examine each equation in turn.

- Equation I has solutions. We have $a=15,$ $b=-20,$ and $c=5.$ Since

$$
d=\text{gcd}(15,-20)=5
$$

and $5\,|\,5,$ our equation has solutions.

- Equation II has solutions. We have $a=11,$ $b=9,$ and $c=13.$ Since

$$
d=\text{gcd}(11,9)=1
$$

and $1\,|\,13,$ our equation has solutions.

- Equation III has no solution. We have $a=-8,$ $b=2,$ and $c=5.$ Since

$$
d=\text{gcd}(-8,2)=2
$$

and $2\,\text{⧸}|\,5,$ our equation has no solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

before.:question/problem:
![](images/5a/5a3961346a4bcb0d94e46caf6d6ed1253dc56fb4761db07b11829e329bc2fa8d.png)

Consider the part of parabola and constant vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be the path where the part of parabola is traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$
- ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$
- ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$

Select all that apply.
before.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements I is false, while statement II is true. As the particle moves from $A$ to $B,$ the force $F$ works against the particle for $x>0,$ while $F$  works with the particle for $x<0.$ 

![](images/af/af80eab6427f376084301c03715fd098cfe4a1c816dcd72d3e1129cfa35ff29d.png)

 

By symmetry, the contribution to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for $x<0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $x>0.$ So,

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/a2/a26ca79400bf30aa891543d30a052a6e8ec071ccb48fcd8c418fe0a713dad212.png)

 

So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

![](images/f7/f712612e5cf628e2cf6f2aac5195bf98b620edee4cab1791829a4ade13bcee15.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above, and let $C$ be the path along the segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
after.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ is true, while statement ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$ is false. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/87/8726ab8c3d764016e1bfa5206769674b6809ab3ea047b03734ae5141f0b553b9.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- Statement ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ is false. It's clear from the picture below that if we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves from $B$ to $A.$

![](images/56/56e77c37324ca2f28c0a09d762d1e5e1f4a29f5f00695e5cbadca748d92b1c6f.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$ only.

before.:question/problem:
Given that $5a≡5b\,(\text{mod}\,15),$ which of the following statements **must** be true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,6)$

- **II.** $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,3)$

- **III.** $4a≡4b\,(\text{mod}\,12)$
before.:question/worked-solution:
The division properties of modular arithmetic state the following:

- For $k\ne 0,$ we have

$$
ka≡kb\,(\text{mod}\,kn)\,⟺\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

- For $\text{gcd}(k,n)=1,$ we have 

$$
ka≡kb\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. Applying the first property, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5a & ≡5b &  & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ 5\cdot a & ≡5\cdot b &  & (\text{mod}\,5\cdot 3) \\ \cancel{5}\cdot a & ≡\cancel{5}\cdot b &  & (\text{mod}\,\cancel{5}\cdot 3) \\ a & ≡b &  & (\text{mod}\,3)\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. By statement II and the first property, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,3)\,⟺\,4a≡4b\,(\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only
."

before.:question/problem:
Consider a vector space $V$ and vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}\in V.$ Given that ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly dependent and ${{v}_{1},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0$ has only zero solution ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}={x}_{4}=0$
- **II.** ${v}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{3}$ and ${v}_{4}$
- **III.** ${v}_{4}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}$
before.:question/worked-solution:
Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is a linearly dependent set, we obtain that

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

has a non-zero solution.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, solving equation ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0$ for ${v}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
{v}_{2}=-\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{x}_{3}}{{x}_{2}}{v}_{3}-\frac{{x}_{4}}{{x}_{2}}{v}_{4}.
$$

Moreover, ${x}_{2}$ can't be zero because then

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}+{x}_{4}{v}_{4}=0
$$

will have a non-zero solution and that's a contradiction as ${{v}_{1},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent.
Hence, ${v}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{3}$ and ${v}_{4}.$

- Statement III is false. Since the set ${{v}_{1},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent set, the equation 

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{3}+{x}_{3}{v}_{4}=0
$$

has no non-zero solution. Hence, ${v}_{4}$ is not a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
